justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an asset trading near the 284–285 level. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last known price, assuming mean-reversion tendencies dominate over very short windows and that no major catalyst was imminent. The slight upward drift in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a small positive carry or trend assumption — markets in the absence of strong contrary signals tend to exhibit slight upward drift, particularly in equity indices or similar instruments. The one-month estimate of 289 represents roughly a 1.5% gain from spot, which is conservative and consistent with historical average monthly returns in calm conditions.

Confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility scaling with the square root of time. At one day, a range of roughly plus or minus 2.5% around the point estimate reflects normal intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, the interval widens to about plus or minus 5.6%, and at one month it reaches roughly plus or minus 11.7% — all broadly consistent with annualized volatility somewhere in the 25–30% range, which is a reasonable baseline for moderately volatile assets. The asymmetry in the intervals is minimal here, reflecting no strong skew assumption in either direction.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected macroeconomic shock — such as a surprise central bank policy shift, deteriorating credit conditions, or a geopolitical escalation — could push prices well below the lower bound of the one-month interval. Liquidity crises or correlated asset selloffs can produce fat-tailed moves that standard volatility-based intervals systematically understate. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data release, a policy pivot toward easing, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above the upper bound.

It's also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively stationary volatility over the forecast horizon, which is itself a fragile assumption. Volatility clustering means that if turbulence begins within the first few days, the actual distribution of one-month outcomes widens considerably beyond what I've stated. Conversely, if conditions remain calm, realized outcomes will likely cluster tightly around the point estimates. The intervals should therefore be treated as unconditional probabilistic ranges, not guarantees, and they carry their own model risk from the assumptions embedded in how I calibrated the volatility inputs.
